author: Paul the apostle, who names himself in 1:1.
recipients: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker and "own son in the faith" (1:2), whom Paul had left to lead the church at Ephesus (1:3).

date.traditional: About AD 62-64, after Paul's first Roman imprisonment and before his second, during travels not recorded in Acts.
date.scholarly: Many critical scholars date the letter later, around AD 80-110, and see it as written in Paul's name by a follower. Others defend Paul's authorship and the earlier date.

writtenFrom: Not stated. Paul had gone on to Macedonia after leaving Timothy in Ephesus (1:3), so he may have written from there.
destination: Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia, known for its great temple of Artemis (Diana; see Acts 19).
purpose: To instruct Timothy on leading the church in Ephesus: confronting false teachers, setting qualifications for elders and deacons, guiding how believers conduct themselves in worship and in the household of God (3:14-15), and encouraging Timothy as a young leader.
setting: Nero was emperor (AD 54-68). The church was spreading across the empire and facing false teaching from within; Nero's persecution of Christians followed the fire of Rome in AD 64.

outline.title: Why Paul writes: conduct in God's household
False teaching identified; how Timothy should lead
Caring for groups in the church: widows, elders, servants
False teachers, contentment, and a final charge

themes: Sound teaching produces godly living; belief and behavior belong together.
God desires all people to be saved (2:4).
Church leaders must be people of proven character.
Everything God created is good and is received with thanksgiving (4:4).
Contentment, and the danger of the love of money (6:6-10).
basis: Restated from Kourtland's 1 Timothy overview notes and the letter's own text; dating views summarized from standard introductions.
